To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

circulating bone marrow-derived Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1-positive hematopoietic stem cells (HPC) and vascular endothelial growth factor-2-positive endothelial progenitor cell (EPC) increase in patients with relapsing breast cancer and metastatic disease, and that these cells decrease in patients with responding disease.

an increase in circulating VEGFR1-expressing hematopoietic cells and VEGRF2-expressing endothelial cells predicts relapse in patients with breast cancer and that an increase in VEGRF1-expressing cells and a decrease in VEGRF2 expressing cells predicts progression of disease in patients with metastatic breast cancer.

the increase of circulating VEGFR1-expressing bone marrow-derived hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSCs) and Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2-expressing bone-marrow-derived endothelial progenitor cell (EPC) levels predict relapse and lack response in patients with breast cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of VEGFR1+/CD34+ HPCs, VEGFR2+/CD133+ EPCs, and VEGF in the pathophysiology of breast cancer metastasis.
identifying biomarkers of breast cancer (BC).
understanding how the tumor microenvironment (TME) affects the behavior of breast cancer (BC).

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of VEGF receptor 1 (Vegfr1) expressing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Vegfr+ HPCs), and VEGFR-2 expressing endothelial progenitor cell (Vegfr2+ EPC), in the peripheral blood of breast cancer (BC), is associated with poor outcome.
